case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The holding is about the CFAA only. It leaves contract, trespass to chattels, copyright and state privacy claims fully available, and LinkedIn later prevailed on contract grounds.
case.holding: Scraping data that a website makes publicly available without any login does not amount to access without authorisation under the CFAA.
case.case_name: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp.

Amazon.com Services LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The principal authority that collecting public web data is not a federal computer crime, which is the first hurdle any web-scale training corpus has to clear.

reading.body:
The Ninth Circuit ruled in 2022 that accessing publicly available website data without a login does not violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, removing a major legal barrier to web-scale data collection for AI training.

This decision established that the CFAA, the federal statute most commonly invoked to block data scraping, does not protect public information simply because a company wishes to restrict access. The holding was narrow, addressing only this statute. Contract law, trespass to chattels, copyright, and state privacy claims remained available to websites as separate grounds for enforcement, and LinkedIn later won its case against hiQ Labs on contract grounds. The decision did not resolve whether scraping violates other laws or whether terms of service can override it.

For AI systems, the ruling matters because training corpora require enormous volumes of text, images, and code harvested from the internet. Any legal theory that criminalized collecting public data would have imposed a hard floor on what systems could legally learn from. This decision removed one such theory from the table. It does not mean web scraping is unregulated, only that it is not a federal computer crime by itself.

What this case does not cover is equally important. It says nothing about whether copyright holders can block training use, whether breach of contract claims will succeed, or whether state laws provide different protections. The live litigation against Perplexity AI by Amazon suggests these remaining theories are actively contested. The precedent clears one legal hurdle. Many others remain in place.
